Here, we consider\nthe molecular recognition of short DNA oligonucleotide single strands. We show\nthat a better matching oligonucleotide strand can prevail against a\ndisproportionally more concentrated competitor that exhibits reduced affinity\ndue to a mismatch. The magnitude of deviation from the simple picture above may\nreach several orders of magnitude. In our experiments the effective molecular\naffinity of a given strand remains elevated only as long as the better matching\ncompetitor is not present. We interpret our observations based on an\nenergy-barrier of entropic origin that occurs if two competing oligonucleotide\nstrands occupy the same probe simultaneously. In this situation the relative\nbinding affinities are reduced asymmetrically, which leads to an expression of\nthe free energy landscape that represents a formal analogue of a Landau\ndescription of phase transitions. Our mean field description reproduces the\nobservations in quantitative agreement. The advantage of improved molecular\nrecognition comes at no energetic cost other than the design of the molecular\nensemble, and the introduction of the competitor. It will be interesting to see\nif mechanisms along similar lines as exposed here, contribute to the molecular\nsynergy that occurs in biological systems.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1602.04722v1', ['Biomolecules'], []]

[u'Hierarchical assembly may be a way to make large information-rich\n  structures', ['Stephen Whitelam'], u'2015-05-27', u"Self-assembly in the laboratory can now yield `information-rich'\nnanostructures in which each component is of a distinct type and has a defined\nspatial position. The chief drawback of this scheme\nis that it is particularly susceptible to kinetic traps that result from\n`non-native' interactions (interactions not required to stabilize the intended\nstructure); the scale on which such a scheme can be realized therefore depends\nupon how effectively this latter kind of interaction can be suppressed.", u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1505.07501v2', ['Biomolecules'], []]

Enhanced sampling approaches, such as\nparallel tempering or umbrella sampling, can accelerate the computation of\nequilibrium expectations massively - but sacrifice the ability to compute\ndynamical expectations. In this work we establish a principle to combine\nknowledge of the equilibrium distribution with kinetics from fast "downhill"\nrelaxation trajectories using reversible Markov models. This approach is\ngeneral as it does not invoke any specific dynamical model, and can provide\naccurate estimates of the rare event kinetics. Large gains in sampling\nefficiency can be achieved whenever one direction of the process occurs more\nrapid than its reverse, making the approach especially attractive for downhill\nprocesses such as folding and binding in biomolecules.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1409.6439v2', ['Biomolecules'], []]

The practical success of such an approach\ndepends very much on the ability to finely discretize the slow order\nparameters. How can this task be achieved in a high-dimensional configuration\nspace without relying on subjective guesses of the slow order parameters? In\nthis paper, we use the variational principle of conformation dynamics to derive\nan optimal way of identifying the "slow subspace" of a large set of prior order\nparameters - either generic internal coordinates (distances and dihedral\nangles), or a user-defined set of parameters. It is shown that a method to\nidentify this slow subspace exists in statistics: the time-lagged independent\ncomponent analysis (TICA). Furthermore, optimal indicators-order parameters\nindicating the progress of the slow transitions and thus may serve as reaction\ncoordinates-are readily identified. We demonstrate that the slow subspace is\nwell suited to construct accurate kinetic models of two sets of molecular\ndynamics simulations, the 6-residue fluorescent peptide MR121-GSGSW and the\n30-residue natively disordered peptide KID. The identified optimal indicators\nreveal the structural changes associated with the slow processes of the\nmolecular system under analysis.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1302.6614v1', ['Biomolecules'], []]

[u'Correlation between nucleotide composition and folding energy of coding\n  sequences with special attention to wobble bases', ['Jan C. This\ncapability is likely to be provided by a physical approach to probing DNA at\nthe single nucleotide level. This is in sharp contrast to current techniques\nand instruments which probe, through chemical elongation, electrophoresis, and\noptical detection, length differences and terminating bases of strands of DNA.\nIn this Colloquium we review several physical approaches to DNA detection that\nhave the potential to deliver fast and low-cost sequencing. Center-fold to\nthese approaches is the concept of nanochannels or nanopores which allow for\nthe spatial confinement of DNA molecules. In addition to their possible impact\nin medicine and biology, the methods offer ideal test beds to study open\nscientific issues and challenges in the relatively unexplored area at the\ninterface between solids, liquids, and biomolecules at the nanometer length\nscale. We emphasize the physics behind these methods and ideas, critically\ndescribe their advantages and drawbacks, and discuss future research\nopportunities in this field.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/0708.2724v1', ['Biomolecules'], []]
[u'Model for processive nucleotide and repeat additions by the telomerase', ['Ping Xie'], u'2007-08-19', u'A model is presented to describe the nucleotide and repeat addition\nprocessivity by the telomerase. In the model, the processive nucleotide\naddition is implemented on the basis of two requirements: One is that stem IV\nloop stimulates the chemical reaction of nucleotide incorporation, and the\nother one is the existence of an ssRNA-binding site adjacent to the polymerase\nsite that has a high affinity for the unpaired base of the template. The\nunpairing of DNA:RNA hybrid after the incorporation of the nucleotide paired\nwith the last base on the template, which is the prerequisite for repeat\naddition processivity, is caused by a force acting on the primer. The force is\nresulted from the unfolding of stem III pseudoknot that is induced by the\nswinging of stem IV loop towards the nucleotide-bound polymerase site. Moreover, some predictions are presented.\nIn particular, it is predicted that the repeat addition processivity is mainly\ndetermined by the difference between the free energy required to disrupt the\nDNA:RNA hybrid and that required to unfold the stem III pseudoknot, with the\nlarge difference corresponding to a low repeat addition processivity while the\nsmall one corresponding to a high repeat addition processivity.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/0708.2527v1', ['Biomolecules'], []]

Reimann', 'Marc-Oliver Gewaltig', 'Wulfram Gerstner', 'Henry Markram', 'Idan Segev', 'Eilif Muller'], u'2016-04-01', u'A method is presented for the reduction of morphologically detailed\nmicrocircuit models to a point-neuron representation without human\nintervention. The simplification occurs in a modular workflow, in the\nneighborhood of a user specified network activity state for the reference\nmodel, the "operating point". First, synapses are moved to the soma, correcting\nfor dendritic filtering by low-pass filtering the delivered synaptic current.\nFilter parameters are computed numerically and independently for inhibitory and\nexcitatory input on the basal and apical dendrites, respectively, in a distance\ndependent and post-synaptic m-type specific manner. Next, point-neuron models\nfor each neuron in the microcircuit are fit to their respective morphologically\ndetailed counterparts. Here, generalized integrate-and-fire point neuron models\nare used, leveraging a recently published fitting toolbox. The fits are\nconstrained by currents and voltages computed in the morphologically detailed\npartner neurons with soma corrected synapses at three depolarizations about the\nuser specified operating point. The result is a simplified circuit which is\nwell constrained by the reference circuit, and can be continuously updated as\nthe latter iteratively integrates new data. The modularity of the approach\nmakes it applicable also for other point-neuron and synapse models. The\napproach is demonstrated on a recently reported reconstruction of a neocortical\nmicrocircuit around an in vivo-like working point. The resulting simplified\nnetwork model is benchmarked to the reference morphologically detailed\nmicrocircuit model for a range of simulated network protocols. The simplified\nnetwork is found to be slightly more sub-critical than the reference, with\notherwise good agreement for both quantitative and qualitative validations.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00087v1', ['Neurons and Cognition'], []]

[u'Mean Time-to-Fire for the Noisy LIF Neuron - A Detailed Derivation of\n  the Siegert Formula', ['Ken Kreutz-Delgado'], u'2015-01-16', u'When stimulated by a very large number of Poisson-like presynaptic current\ninput spikes, the temporal dynamics of the soma membrane potential $V(t)$ of a\nleaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron is typically modeled in the diffusion\nlimit and treated as a Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process (OUP). When the potential\nreaches a threshold value $\\theta$, $V(t) = \\theta$, the LIF neuron fires and\nthe membrane potential is reset to a resting value, $V_0 < \\theta$, and clamped\nto this value for a specified (non-stochastic) absolute refractory period $T_r\n\\ge 0$, after which the cycle is repeated. The time between firings is given by\nthe random variable $T_f = T_r+ T$ where $T$ is the random time which elapses\nbetween the "unpinning" of the membrane potential clamp and the next,\nsubsequent firing of the neuron. The mean time-to-fire, $\\widehat{T}_f =\n\\text{E}(T_f) = T_r + \\text{E}(T) = T_r + \\widehat{T}$, provides a measure\n$\\rho$ of the average firing rate of the neuron, \\[ \\rho = \\widehat{T}_f^{-1} =\n\\frac{1}{T_r + \\widehat{T}} . \\] This note briefly discusses some aspects of\nthe OUP model and derives the Siegert formula giving the firing rate, $\\rho =\n\\rho(I_0)$ as a function of an injected current, $I_0$. This is a well-known\nclassical result and no claim to originality is made. The derivation of the\nfiring rate given in this report, which closely follows the derivation outlined\nin the textbook by Gardiner, minimizes the required mathematical background and\nis done in some pedagogic detail to facilitate study by graduate students and\nothers who are new to the subject. Introducing a leader that broadcasts its actions\nthroughout the population increases the fitness of actions but reduces\ndiversity of actions. [u"Pairwise maximum entropy models for studying large biological systems:\n  when they can and when they can't work", ['Yasser Roudi', 'Sheila Nirenberg', 'Peter Latham'], u'2008-11-06', u'One of the most critical problems we face in the study of biological systems\nis building accurate statistical descriptions of them. This problem has been\nparticularly challenging because biological systems typically contain large\nnumbers of interacting elements, which precludes the use of standard brute\nforce approaches. Recently, though, several groups have reported that there may\nbe an alternate strategy. The reports show that reliable statistical models can\nbe built without knowledge of all the interactions in a system; instead,\npairwise interactions can suffice. These findings, however, are based on the\nanalysis of small subsystems. Here we ask whether the observations will\ngeneralize to systems of realistic size, that is, whether pairwise models will\nprovide reliable descriptions of true biological systems. If the size is above the crossover point, the results do have\npredictive power. This work thus provides a general framework for determining\nthe extent to which pairwise models can be used to predict the behavior of\nwhole biological systems. Applied to neural data, the size of most systems\nstudied so far is below the crossover point.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/0811.0903v1', ['Neurons and Cognition', 'Quantitative Methods'], []]

Unrooted phylogenetic networks form a\nspecial class of such networks, which naturally generalize unrooted\nphylogenetic trees. In this paper we define two operations on unrooted\nphylogenetic networks, one of which is a generalization of the well-known\nnearest-neighbor interchange (NNI) operation on phylogenetic trees. We show\nthat any unrooted phylogenetic network can be transformed into any other such\nnetwork using only these operations. This generalizes the well-known fact that\nany phylogenetic tree can be transformed into any other such tree using only\nNNI operations. It also allows us to define a generalization of tree space and\nto define some new metrics on unrooted phylogenetic networks. To prove our main\nresults, we employ some fascinating new connections between phylogenetic\nnetworks and cubic graphs that we have recently discovered. Our results should\nbe useful in developing new strategies to search for optimal phylogenetic\nnetworks, a topic that has recently generated some interest in the literature,\nas well as for providing new ways to compare networks.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1601.01788v1', ['Populations and Evolution'], []]

At each step of the discrete-time\nprocess, an individual is chosen with probability proportional to its fitness,\nand its state (mutant or non-mutant) is passed on to an out-neighbour chosen\nu.a.r. We define an infinite family of directed graphs to be\nstrongly amplifying if, for every $r>1$, the extinction probability tends to 0\nas the number $n$ of vertices increases. Strong amplification is a rather\nsurprising property - the initial mutant only has a fixed selective advantage,\nindependent of $n$, which is "amplified" to give a fixation probability tending\nto 1. Strong amplifiers have received quite a bit of attention. Lieberman et\nal. proposed two potential families of them: superstars and metafunnels. It has\nbeen argued heuristically that some infinite families of superstars are\nstrongly amplifying. The same has been claimed for metafunnels. We give the\nfirst rigorous proof that there is a strongly amplifying family of directed\ngraphs which we call "megastars". We show that the extinction probability of\n$n$-vertex graphs in this family of megastars is roughly $n^{-1/2}$, up to\nlogarithmic factors, and that all infinite families of superstars and\nmetafunnels have larger extinction probabilities as a function of $n$. Our\nanalysis of megastars is tight, up to logarithmic factors. We also clarify the\nliterature on the isothermal theorem of Lieberman et al.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1512.05632v1', ['Populations and Evolution'], []]

In\nthese examples, each atomistic decision, at a point in time, of the better-off\nentity to cooperate poses a puzzle: the better-off entity will book an\nimmediate net loss -- why should it cooperate? For each example, specific\nexplanations have been put forward. Here we point out a very general mechanism\n-- a sufficient null model -- whereby cooperation can evolve. The mechanism is\nbased the following insight: natural growth processes tend to be\nmultiplicative. In multiplicative growth, ergodicity is broken in such a way\nthat fluctuations have a net-negative effect on the time-average growth rate,\nalthough they have no effect on the growth rate of the ensemble average.\nPooling and sharing resources reduces fluctuations, which leaves ensemble\naverages unchanged but -- contrary to common perception -- increases the\ntime-average growth rate for each cooperator.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1506.03414v1', ['Populations and Evolution'], []]

Fraser'], u'2013-08-07', u'Despite recent advances in our ability to detect adaptive evolution involving\nthe cis-regulation of gene expression, our knowledge of the molecular\nmechanisms underlying these adaptations has lagged far behind. Across all model\norganisms the causal mutations have been discovered for only a handful of gene\nexpression adaptations, and even for these, mechanistic details (e.g. the\ntrans-regulatory factors involved) have not been determined. Pruning the\nextinct lineages out of such trees leads to natural models for reconstructed\ntrees (i.e., phylogenies of extant species). Alternatively, reconstructed trees\ncan be modelled by coalescent point processes (CPP), where trees grow\n"horizontally" by the sequential addition of vertical edges. Each new edge\nstarts at some random speciation time and ends at the present time; speciation\ntimes are drawn from the same distribution independently. CPP lead to extremely\nfast computation of tree likelihoods and simulation of reconstructed trees.\nTheir topology always follows the uniform distribution on ranked tree shapes\n(URT). If rates additionally depend on the number of species,\nthe reconstructed tree is (only) URT (but not CPP). We characterize the common\ndistribution of speciation times in the CPP description, and discuss incomplete\nspecies sampling as well as three special model cases in detail: 1) extinction\nrate does not depend on a trait; 2) rates do not depend on time; 3) mass\nextinctions may happen additionally at certain points in the past.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1308.1289v1', ['Populations and Evolution'], []]

In fact, the limiting coalescent\nmodel under a high rate of sweeps to low frequency is identical to the standard\nneutral model. [u'A general model of the public goods dilemma', ['Steven A. Moreover, in large groups the presence\nof a small number of defectors is bearable, which makes the mixed phase region\nexpand with increasing group size. [u'Maladaptation and the paradox of robustness in evolution', ['Steven A. Frank'], u'2011-12-13', u'Background. Organisms use a variety of mechanisms to protect themselves\nagainst perturbations. For example, repair mechanisms fix damage, feedback\nloops keep homeostatic systems at their setpoints, and biochemical filters\ndistinguish signal from noise. Such buffering mechanisms are often discussed in\nterms of robustness, which may be measured by reduced sensitivity of\nperformance to perturbations. Methodology/Principal Findings. I use a\nmathematical model to analyze the evolutionary dynamics of robustness in order\nto understand aspects of organismal design by natural selection. I focus on two\ncharacters: one character performs an adaptive task; the other character\nbuffers the performance of the first character against perturbations. Increased\nperturbations favor enhanced buffering and robustness, which in turn decreases\nsensitivity and reduces the intensity of natural selection on the adaptive\ncharacter. Reduced selective pressure on the adaptive character often leads to\na less costly, lower performance trait. Conclusions/Significance. The paradox\nof robustness arises from evolutionary dynamics: enhanced robustness causes an\nevolutionary reduction in the adaptive performance of the target character,\nleading to a degree of maladaptation compared to what could be achieved by\nnatural selection in the absence of robustness mechanisms. Over evolutionary\ntime, buffering traits may become layered on top of each other, while the\nunderlying adaptive traits become replaced by cheaper, lower performance\ncomponents. The paradox of robustness has widespread implications for\nunderstanding organismal design.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1112.2933v1', ['Populations and Evolution', 'Molecular Networks'], []]

By contrast,\nFisher believed that fluctuating selection in large populations was the main\ncause of fluctuation in nonadditive gene combinations. We\nshow that for a certain range of the parameter $k$ both models exhibit an\noscillatory phase in a region of parameter space that corresponds to weak\ndriving. For\n$k=3, 4$, we compare the phase diagram of the standard pair approximation\nequations of both models with the results of simulations on regular random\ngraphs of the same degree. We show that for parameter values in the oscillatory\nphase, and even for large system sizes, the simulations either die out or\nexhibit damped oscillations, depending on the initial conditions. We discuss\nthis failure of the standard pair approximation model to capture even the\nqualitative behavior of the simulations on large regular random graphs and the\nrelevance of the oscillatory phase in the pair approximation diagrams to\nexplain the cycling behavior found in real populations.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/0907.0335v2', ['Populations and Evolution'], []]
[u'Extinction of metastable stochastic populations', ['Michael Assaf', 'Baruch Meerson'], u'2009-07-01', u'We investigate extinction of a long-lived self-regulating stochastic\npopulation, caused by intrinsic (demographic) noise. Extinction typically\noccurs via one of two scenarios depending on whether the absorbing state n=0 is\na repelling (scenario A) or attracting (scenario B) point of the deterministic\nrate equation. In scenario A the metastable stochastic population resides in\nthe vicinity of an attracting fixed point next to the repelling point n=0. In\nscenario B there is an intermediate repelling point n=n_1 between the\nattracting point n=0 and another attracting point n=n_2 in the vicinity of\nwhich the metastable population resides. The crux of the theory is WKB method\nwhich assumes that the typical population size in the metastable state is\nlarge. Starting from the master equation, we calculate the quasi-stationary\nprobability distribution of the population sizes and the (exponentially long)\nmean time to extinction for each of the two scenarios. When necessary, the WKB\napproximation is complemented (i) by a recursive solution of the\nquasi-stationary master equation at small n and (ii) by the van Kampen\nsystem-size expansion, valid near the fixed points of the deterministic rate\nequation. The theory yields both entropic barriers to extinction and\npre-exponential factors, and holds for a general set of multi-step processes\nwhen detailed balance is broken. The results simplify considerably for\nsingle-step processes and near the characteristic bifurcations of scenarios A\nand B.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/0907.0070v3', ['Populations and Evolution'], []]

In principle, confining $d$ distinct templates of\nlength $L$ in a package or protocell, whose survival depends on the coexistence\nof the templates it holds in, could resolve this crisis provided that $d$ is\nmade sufficiently large. Here we review the prototypical package model of\nNiesert et al. 1981 which guarantees the greatest possible region of viability\nof the protocell population, and show that this model, and hence the entire\npackage approach, does not resolve the information crisis. Such non-transitive relations lead to an evolution\nwith central features represented by the `rock-paper-scissors' game, where rock\ncrushes scissors, scissors cut paper, and paper wraps rock. In combination with\nspatial dispersal of static populations, this type of competition results in\nthe stable coexistence of all species and the long-term maintenance of\nbiodiversity. However, population mobility is a central feature of real\necosystems: animals migrate, bacteria run and tumble. Here, we observe a\ncritical influence of mobility on species diversity. When mobility exceeds a\ncertain value, biodiversity is jeopardized and lost. In contrast, below this\ncritical threshold all subpopulations coexist and an entanglement of travelling\nspiral waves forms in the course of temporal evolution. We establish that this\nphenomenon is robust, it does not depend on the details of cyclic competition\nor spatial environment. These findings have important implications for\nmaintenance and evolution of ecological systems and are relevant for the\nformation and propagation of patterns in excitable media, such as chemical\nkinetics or epidemic outbreaks.", u'http://arxiv.org/abs/0709.0217v2', ['Populations and Evolution'], []]

The theoretical tool used is the\nFokker-Planck equation, its characteristic quantities being the diffusion\nconstant which describes the motion of the animals, and the attractive\npotential which addresses their tendency to live near their burrows. The\nmeasurement technique is shown to correspond to the calculation of a certain\nkind of mean square displacement of the animals relevant to the specific\nprobing window in space corresponding to the trapping region. The output of the\ntheory is a sigmoid curve of the observable mean square displacement as a\nfunction of the ratio of distances characteristic of the home range and the\ntrapping region, along with an explicit prescription to extract the home range\nform observations. Applications of the theory to rodent movement in Panama and\nNew Mexico are pointed out. An analysis is given of the sensitivity of our\ntheory to the choice of the confining potential via the use of various\nrepresentative cases. A comparison is provided between home range size inferred\nfrom our method and from other procedures employed in the literature.\nConsequences of home range overlap are also discussed.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/q-bio/0511026v1', ['Populations and Evolution', 'Other'], []]

Reaction-diffusion models are a bridge between\nmacroscopic and microscopic worlds as they produce mean-field approximations of\nsingle-cell behaviors. Microscopic models describe intracellular events, such\nas branching, septation and translocation. Finally, completely discrete models,\ncellular automata, simulate the microscopic interaction among cells to\nreproduce emergent cooperative behaviors of large colonies. In this comment, we\nreview a selection of models for each of these length scales, stressing their\nadvantages and shortcomings.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/q-bio/0402004v1', ['Populations and Evolution', 'Cell Behavior'], []]

[u'Mass Action and Conservation of Current', ['Bob Eisenberg'], u'2015-02-25', u'The law of mass action is used widely. All the 20 chiral amino acids in the levo form used in the proteins\nof the current terrestrial biochemistry have been irradiated in the solid state\nwith gamma radiation to a dose of 3.2 MGy which is the dose equivalent to that\nderived by radionuclide decay in comets and asteroids in 1.05x109 years. For\neach amino acid the radiolysis degree and the radioracemization degree was\nmeasured by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and by optical rotatory\ndispersion (ORD) spectroscopy. From these measurements a radiolysis rate\nconstant kdsc and a radioracemization rate constant krac have been determined\nfor each amino acid and extrapolated to a dose of 14 MGy which corresponds to\nthe expected total dose delivered by the natural radionuclides decay to all the\norganic molecules present in comets and asteroids in 4.6x109 years, the age of\nthe Solar System. It is shown that all the amino acids studied can survive a\nradiation dose of 14 MGy in significant quantity although part of them are lost\nin radiolytic processes. Similarly, also the radioracemization process\naccompanying the radiolysis does not extinguish the chirality. The knowledge of\nthe radiolysis and radioracemization rate constants may permit the calculation\nof the original concentration of the amino acids at the times of the formation\nof the Solar System starting from the concentration found today in carbonaceous\nchondrites. For some amino acids the concentration in the presolar nebula could\nhave been up to 6 times higher than currently observed in meteorites.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1007.4529v1', ['Other'], []]

Biological applications\nof impedance spectroscopy are often not useful since so much of biology is\nstrongly nonlinear in its essential features, and impedance spectroscopy is\nfundamentally a linear analysis. In the lens of the eye, impedance spectroscopy changed\nthe basis of all recording and interpretation of electrical measurements and\nlaid the basis for Rae and Mathias extensive later experimental work. Many\ntissues are riddled with extracellular space as clefts and tubules, for\nexample, cardiac muscle, the lens of the eye, most epithelia, and of course\nfrog muscle. These tissues are best analyzed with a bidomain theory that arose\nfrom the work on electrical structure described here. This enables researchers to quantitatively infer the magnitude\nand directionality of forces experienced by biomolecules in their native\ncellular environments. Situations where such forces are biologically relevant\nrange from mitosis to directed transport of protein cargo along cytoskeletal\nstructures. Models commonly applied to quantify single-molecule dynamics assume\nthat effective forces and velocity in the $x,y$ (or $x,y,z$) directions are\nstatistically independent, but this assumption is physically unrealistic in\nmany situations. We present a hypothesis testing approach capable of\ndetermining if there is evidence of statistical dependence between positional\ncoordinates in experimentally measured trajectories; if the hypothesis of\nindependence between spatial coordinates is rejected, then a new model\naccounting for 2D (3D) interactions should be considered to more faithfully\nrepresent the underlying experimental kinetics. The technique is robust in the\nsense that 2D (3D) interactions can be detected via statistical hypothesis\ntesting even if there is substantial inconsistency between the physical\nparticle\'s actual noise sources and the simplified model\'s assumed noise\nstructure. For example, 2D (3D) interactions can be reliably detected even if\nthe researcher assumes normal diffusion, but the experimental data experiences\n"anomalous diffusion" and/or is subjected to a measurement noise characterized\nby a distribution differing from that assumed by the fitted model. The approach\nis demonstrated on control simulations and on experimental data (IFT88 directed\ntransport in the primary cilium).', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6742v1', ['Quantitative Methods'], []]

Traditionally such networks were modeled\ndeterministically, but it is now well-established that when reactant copy\nnumbers are small, the random timing of the reactions create internal noise\nthat can significantly affect the macroscopic properties of the system. To\nunderstand the role of noise and quantify its effects, stochastic models are\nnecessary. In the stochastic setting, the population is described by a\nprobability distribution, which evolves according to a set of ordinary\ndifferential equations known as the Chemical Master Equation (CME). This set is\ninfinite in most cases making the CME practically unsolvable. In many\napplications, it is important to determine if the solution of a CME has a\nglobally attracting fixed point. This property is called ergodicity and its\npresence leads to several important insights about the underlying dynamics. This litter-to-litter variation, or "litter\neffects", can influence the results in addition to the experimental factors of\ninterest. Furthermore, an experimental treatment can be applied to whole\nlitters rather than to individual offspring. For example, in the valproic acid\n(VPA) model of autism, VPA is administered to pregnant females thereby inducing\nthe disease phenotype in the offspring. With this type of experiment the sample\nsize is the number of litters and not the total number of offspring. If such\nexperiments are not appropriately designed and analysed, the results can be\nseverely biased as well as extremely underpowered.\n  Results: A review of the VPA literature showed that only 9% (3/34) of studies\ncorrectly determined that the experimental unit (n) was the litter and\ntherefore made valid statistical inferences. In addition, litter effects\naccounted for up to 61% (p <0.001) of the variation in behavioural outcomes,\nwhich was larger than the treatment effects. In addition, few studies reported\nusing randomisation (12%) or blinding (18%), and none indicated that a sample\nsize calculation or power analysis had been conducted.\n  Conclusions: Litter effects are common, large, and ignoring them can make\nreplication of findings difficult and can contribute to the low rate of\ntranslating preclinical in vivo studies into successful therapies. Only a\nminority of studies reported using rigorous experimental methods, which is\nconsistent with much of the preclinical in vivo literature.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1211.7320v2', ['Quantitative Methods'], []]

It is in general prohibitive\nto enumerate all EFMs for complex networks, since the number of EFMs increases\nrapidly with network complexity. In this work we present an optimization-based\nmethod that dynamically generates a subset of EFMs and solves the EFMs-based\nMFA problem simultaneously. The obtained subset contains EFMs that contribute\nto the optimal solution of the EFMs-based MFA problem. The usefulness of our\nmethod was examined in a case-study using data from a Chinese hamster ovary\ncell culture and two networks of varied complexity. It was demonstrated that\nthe EFMs-based MFA problem could be solved at a low computational cost, even\nfor the more complex network. Additionally, only a fraction of the total number\nof EFMs was needed to compute the optimal solution.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1410.2680v1', ['Molecular Networks'], []]

Emrah Nikerel', 'Domenico Bellomo'], u'2011-09-25', u'RNA thermometers are mRNA strands with a temperature dependent secondary\nstructure: depending on the spatial conformation, the mRNA strand can get\ntranslated (on-state) or can be inaccessible for ribosomes binding (off-state).\nThese have been found in a number of microorganisms (mainly pathogens), where\nthey are used to adaptively regulate the gene expression, in response to\nchanges in the environmental temperature. Besides naturally occurring RNA\nthermometers, synthetic RNA thermometers have been recently designed by\nmodifying their natural counterparts (Hofacker et al., 2003). The newly\ndesigned RNA thermometers are simpler, and exhibit a sharper switching between\noff- and on-states. However, the proposed trial-and-error design procedure has\nnot been algorithmically formalized, and the switching temperature is rigidly\ndetermined by the natural RNA thermometer used as template for the design.\n  We developed a general algorithmic procedure (consensus distribution) for the\ndesign of RNA thermo-switches with a tunable switching temperature that can be\ndecided in advance by the designer. A software tool with a user friendly GUI\nhas been written to automate the design of RNA thermo-switches with a desired\nthreshold temperature. Starting from a natural template, a new RNA thermometer\nhas been designed by our method for a new desired threshold temperature of 32C.\nThe designed RNA thermo-switch has been experimentally validated by using it to\ncontrol the expression of lucifarase. A 9.2 fold increase of luminescence has\nbeen observed between 30C and 37C, whereas between 20C and 30C the luminescence\nincrease is less than 3-fold.\n  This work represents a first step towards the design of flexible and tunable\nRNA thermometers that can be used for a precise control of gene expression\nwithout the need of external chemicals and possibly for temperature\nmeasurements at a nano-scale resolution.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1109.5402v1', ['Subcellular Processes'], []]

Here we analyse\nthe evolutionary dynamics of non-linear social dilemmas in settings where the\npopulation fluctuates in size and the environment changes over time. In\nparticular, cooperation is often supported and maintained at high densities\nthrough ecological fluctuations. The\nfirst possibility corresponds to an ideal-free distribution, while the second\npossibility corresponds to a "source-sink" spatial structure. By exploiting the problem structure, we model\nreaction recovery as a hyperlink prediction problem, where each reaction is\nregarded as a hyperlink connecting its participating vertices (metabolites).\nDifferent from the traditional link prediction problem where two nodes form a\nlink, a hyperlink can involve an arbitrary number of nodes. Since the\ncardinality of a hyperlink is variable, existing classifiers based on a fixed\nnumber of input features become infeasible. Traditional methods, such as common\nneighbors and Katz index, are not applicable either, since they are restricted\nto pairwise similarities. In this paper, we propose a novel hyperlink\nprediction algorithm, called Matrix Boosting (MATBoost). MATBoost conducts\ninference jointly in the incidence space and adjacency space by performing an\niterative completion-matching optimization. We carry out extensive experiments\nto show that MATBoost achieves state-of-the-art performance. For a metabolic\nnetwork with 1805 metabolites and 2583 reactions, our algorithm can\nsuccessfully recover nearly 200 reactions out of 400 missing reactions.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1610.06941v1', ['Molecular Networks'], []]

Lizier'], u'2016-10-26', u'Transfer entropy has been used to quantify the directed flow of information\nbetween source and target variables in many complex systems. Originally\nformulated in discrete time, we provide a framework for considering transfer\nentropy in continuous time systems. By appealing to a measure theoretic\nformulation we generalise transfer entropy, describing it in terms of\nRadon-Nikodym derivatives between measures of complete path realisations. The\nresulting formalism introduces and emphasises the idea that transfer entropy is\nan expectation of an individually fluctuating quantity along a path, in the\nsame way we consider the expectation of physical quantities such as work and\nheat. We applied a walking identification algorithm to the data and defined features of walking, such as participant-specific walking acceleration and cadence. The association between these walking features and physical function, mobility, fatigability, and fitness was quantified using linear regression analysis. Results. Micro-scale features of walking (acceleration and cadence) estimated from in-the-lab and in-the-wild data were associated with measures of physical function, mobility, fatigability, and fitness. In-the-lab median walking acceleration was strongly inversely associated with physical function, mobility, fatigability and fitness. Additionally, in-the-wild daily walking time was inversely associated with usual- and fast-paced 400m walking time. Conclusions. It is an interesting feature of Fokker-Planck diffusion that for spatially varying diffusion coefficients the stationary solution is not a homogeneous distribution; in contrast to Fickian diffusion. Instead, concentration accumulates in regions of low diffusivity and tends to lower levels for areas of high diffusivity. While classical differential expression analysis provides specific and hence targetable gene-level insights, it does not include any systems--level information. On the other hand, pathway analyses integrate systems--level information with expression data, but are often limited in their ability to indicate specific molecular targets. We introduce GeneSurrounder, an analysis method that takes into account the complex structure of interaction networks to identify specific genes that disrupt pathway activity in a disease--specific manner. GeneSurrounder integrates transcriptomic data and pathway network information in a novel two--step procedure to detect genes that (i) appear to influence the expression of other genes local to it in the network and (ii) are part of a subnetwork of differentially expressed genes. Combined, this evidence can be used to pinpoint specific genes that have a mechanistic role in the phenotype of interest. Applying GeneSurrounder to three distinct ovarian cancer studies using a global KEGG network, we show that our method is able to identify biologically relevant genes and genes missed by single-gene association tests, integrate pathway and expression data, and yield more consistent results across multiple studies of the same phenotype than competing methods.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1705.10922v1', ['Quantitative Methods', 'Molecular Networks', 'Genomics'], []]

We focus on tradeoffs between computation time and network complexity, along with the role of randomness in efficient neural computation. It is widely accepted that neural computation is inherently stochastic. In recent work, we explored how this stochasticity could be leveraged to solve the `winner-take-all' leader election task. Here, we focus on using randomness in neural algorithms for similarity testing and compression. In the most basic setting, given two $n$-length patterns of firing neurons, we wish to distinguish if the patterns are equal or $\\epsilon$-far from equal. Randomization allows us to solve this task with a very compact network, using $O \\left (\\frac{\\sqrt{n}\\log n}{\\epsilon}\\right)$ auxiliary neurons, which is sublinear in the input size. At the heart of our solution is the design of a $t$-round neural random access memory, or indexing network, which we call a neuro-RAM. This module can be implemented with $O(n/t)$ auxiliary neurons and is useful in many applications beyond similarity testing. Using a combination of Yao's minimax principle and a VC dimension-based argument, we show that the tradeoff between runtime and network size in our neuro-RAM is nearly optimal. Our result has several implications -- since our neuro-RAM construction can be implemented with deterministic threshold gates, it demonstrates that, in contrast to similarity testing, randomness does not provide significant computational advantages for this problem. However, in many cases evolution is not treelike and thus, phylogenetic networks have come to the fore as a generalization of phylogenetic trees, allowing for the representation of non-treelike evolutionary events, such as horizontal gene transfer or hybridization. Here, we extend the concepts of phylogenetic diversity and phylogenetic diversity indices from phylogenetic trees to phylogenetic networks. On the one hand, we consider the treelike content of a phylogenetic network, e.g. the (multi)set of phylogenetic trees displayed by a network and the LSA tree associated with it. On the other hand, we derive the phylogenetic diversity of subsets of taxa and biodiversity indices directly from the internal structure of the network. Furthermore, we introduce our software package NetDiversity, which was implemented in Perl and allows for the calculation of all generalized measures of phylogenetic diversity and generalized phylogenetic diversity indices established in this note. [u'The thermodynamic efficiency of computations made in cells across the range of life', ['Christopher P. Moreover, ever since Landauer's bound was proposed it has been known that all computation has some thermodynamic cost -- and that the same computation can be achieved with greater or smaller thermodynamic cost depending on how it is implemented. Accordingly an important issue concerning the evolution of life is assessing the thermodynamic efficiency of the computations performed by organisms. This issue is interesting both from the perspective of how close life has come to maximally efficient computation (presumably under the pressure of natural selection), and from the practical perspective of what efficiencies we might hope that engineered biological computers might achieve, especially in comparison with current computational systems. Here we show that the computational efficiency of translation, defined as free energy expended per amino acid operation, outperforms the best supercomputers by several orders of magnitude, and is only about an order of magnitude worse than the Landauer bound. However this efficiency depends strongly on the size and architecture of the cell in question. In particular, we show that the {\\it useful} efficiency of an amino acid operation, defined as the bulk energy per amino acid polymerization, decreases for increasing bacterial size and converges to the polymerization cost of the ribosome. This cost of the largest bacteria does not change in cells as we progress through the major evolutionary shifts to both single and multicellular eukaryotes. However, the rates of total computation per unit mass are nonmonotonic in bacteria with increasing cell size, and also change across different biological architectures including the shift from unicellular to multicellular eukaryotes.", u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1706.05043v1', ['Other'], []]

All three schemes evolve the state of a neuron through a series of checkpoints: equally spaced in the first scheme and determined neuron-wise by spike events in the latter two. The time-driven and the hybrid scheme determine whether the membrane potential of a neuron crosses a threshold at the end of of the time interval between consecutive checkpoints. Threshold crossing can, however, occur within the interval even if this test is negative. Spikes can therefore be missed. The present work derives, implements, and benchmarks a method for perfect retrospective spike detection. This method can be applied to neuron models with affine or linear subthreshold dynamics. The idea behind the method is to propagate the threshold with a time-inverted dynamics, testing whether the threshold crosses the neuron state to be evolved, rather than vice versa. Algebraically this translates into a set of inequalities necessary and sufficient for threshold crossing. This test is slower than the imperfect one, but faster than an alternative perfect tests based on bisection or root-finding methods. Comparison confirms earlier results that the imperfect test rarely misses spikes (less than a fraction $1/10^8$ of missed spikes) in biologically relevant settings. This study offers an alternative geometric point of view on neuronal dynamics.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1706.05702v1', ['Neurons and Cognition', 'Quantitative Methods'], []]

Scientific and clinical studies must to incorporate datasets that cross multiple spatial and temporal scales to describe a particular phenomenon. The storage and accessibility of these heterogeneous datasets in a way that is useful to researchers and yet extensible to new data types is a major challenge. Methods: In order to overcome these obstacles, we propose the use of data primitives as a common currency between analytical methods. The four data primitives we have identified are time series, text, annotated graph and triangulated mesh, with associated metadata. Using only data primitives to store data and as algorithm input, output, and intermediate results, promotes interoperability, scalability, and reproducibility in scientific studies. Results: Data primitives were used in a multi-omic, multi-scale systems biology study of malaria infection in non-human primates to perform many types of integrative analysis quickly and efficiently. Conclusions: Using data primitives as a common currency for both data storage and for cross talk between analytical methods enables the analysis of complex multi-omic, multi-scale datasets in a reproducible modular fashion.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08131v1', ['Quantitative Methods'], []]

[u'Flows, scaling, and the control of moment hierarchies for stochastic chemical reaction networks', ['Eric Smith', 'Supriya Krishnamurthy'], u'2017-06-23', u'Stochastic chemical reaction networks (CRNs) are complex systems which combine the features of concurrent transformation of multiple variables in each elementary reaction event, and nonlinear relations between states and their rates of change. Most general results concerning CRNs are limited to restricted cases where a topological characteristic known as deficiency takes value 0 or 1. Here we derive equations of motion for fluctuation moments at all orders for stochastic CRNs at general deficiency. We show, for the case of the mass-action rate law, that the generator of the stochastic process acts on the hierarchy of factorial moments with a finite representation. Whereas simulation of high-order moments for many-particle systems is costly, this representation reduces solution of moment hierarchies to a complexity comparable to solving a heat equation. At steady states, moment hierarchies for finite CRNs interpolate between low-order and high-order scaling regimes, which may be approximated separately by distributions similar to those for deficiency-0 networks, and connected through matched asymptotic expansions. In CRNs with multiple stable or metastable steady states, boundedness of high-order moments provides the starting condition for recursive solution downward to low-order moments, reversing the order usually used to solve moment hierarchies. A basis for a subset of network flows defined by having the same mean-regressing property as the flows in deficiency-0 networks gives the leading contribution to low-order moments in CRNs at general deficiency, in a $1/n$-expansion in large particle numbers. Our results give a physical picture of the different informational roles of mean-regressing and non-mean-regressing flows, and clarify the dynamical meaning of deficiency not only for first-moment conditions but for all orders in fluctuations.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08386v1', ['Molecular Networks'], []]

[u'When Neurons Fail', ['El Mahdi El Mhamdi', 'Rachid Guerraoui'], u'2017-06-27', u'We view a neural network as a distributed system of which neurons can fail independently, and we evaluate its robustness in the absence of any (recovery) learning phase. We give tight bounds on the number of neurons that can fail without harming the result of a computation. To determine our bounds, we leverage the fact that neural activation functions are Lipschitz-continuous. Our bound is on a quantity, we call the \\textit{Forward Error Propagation}, capturing how much error is propagated by a neural network when a given number of components is failing, computing this quantity only requires looking at the topology of the network, while experimentally assessing the robustness of a network requires the costly experiment of looking at all the possible inputs and testing all the possible configurations of the network corresponding to different failure situations, facing a discouraging combinatorial explosion. We distinguish the case of neurons that can fail and stop their activity (crashed neurons) from the case of neurons that can fail by transmitting arbitrary values (Byzantine neurons). Interestingly, as we show in the paper, our bound can easily be extended to the case where synapses can fail. We show how our bound can be leveraged to quantify the effect of memory cost reduction on the accuracy of a neural network, to estimate the amount of information any neuron needs from its preceding layer, enabling thereby a boosting scheme that prevents neurons from waiting for unnecessary signals. The habitat is one-dimensional and unbounded, selection at each locus is modeled by step functions such that in one region one allele at each locus is advantageous and in the other deleterious. We admit an environmentally independent, intermediate degree of dominance at both loci, including complete dominance. First, we derive an explicit expression for the single-locus cline with dominance, thus generalizing classical results by Haldane (1948). We show that the slope of the cline in the center (at the step) or, equivalently, the width of the cline, is independent of the degree of dominance. Second, under the assumption of strong recombination relative to selection and migration, the first-order approximations of the allele-frequency clines at each of the loci and of the linkage disequilibrium are derived. This may be interpreted as the quasi-linkage-equilibrium approximation of the two-locus cline. Explicit asymptotic expressions for the clines are deduced as $x\\to\\pm\\infty$. For equivalent loci, explicit expressions for the whole clines are derived. The influence of dominance and of linkage on the slope of the cline in the center and on a global measure of steepness are investigated. This global measure reflects the influence of dominance. Finally, the accuracy of the approximations and the dependence of the shape of the two-locus cline on the full range of recombination rates is explored by numerical integration of the underlying system of partial differential equations.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1708.03499v1', ['Populations and Evolution'], []]

Here, we analyze how motion of individuals affects constant selection in structured populations. We describe motion as the swapping of individuals on graphs, and more generally as the shuffling of individuals between reproductive updates. Beginning with a one-dimensional graph, the cycle, we prove that motion suppresses natural selection for death-birth updating or for any process that combines birth-death and death-birth updating. [u'In reply to Faes et al. and Barnett et al. regarding "A study of problems encountered in Granger causality analysis from a neuroscience perspective"', ['Patrick A. Stokes', 'Patrick L. (PNAS 114(34):7063-7072. 2017). In our paper, we analyzed several properties of Granger-Geweke causality (GGC) and discussed potential problems in neuroscience applications. We demonstrated: (i) that GGC, estimated using separate model fits, is either severely biased, particularly when the true model is known, or a high variance is introduced to overcome the bias; and (ii) that GGC does not reflect some component dynamics of the system. The commentaries by both Faes et al. and Barnett et al. point out that the computational problems of (i) are resolved by using recent computational methods. We acknowledge that these problems are indeed resolved by these methods. However, the traditional computation using separate model fits continues to be presented and applied. More fundamentally, the interpretational problems stemming from (ii) are not in anyway addressed by the improved methods because they are inherent to the definition of GGC. These properties are indeed acknowledged by both commentaries. We have no misconception of the GGC measure and do not claim that these properties are facially wrong. But we do discuss at length how these properties make it inappropriate and misleading for common types of scientific questions, how presentation of GGC results without model estimates are not decipherable, and how the absence of clear statements of questions of interest present further opportunities for misinterpretation.', u'http://arxiv.org/abs/1709.10248v1', ['Neurons and Cognition'], []]

Meaning that at a temperature greater than the folding temperature, the enhanced friction from the hydrodynamic solvents between the beads in an unfolded configuration results in lowered folding rate; conversely, at a temperature lower than the folding temperature, HI accelerates folding by the backflow of solvent toward the native folded state. Additionally, the extent of acceleration depends on the topology of a protein: for a protein like CI2, where its folding nucleus is rather diffuse in a transition state, HI channels the formation of contacts by favoring a major folding pathway in a complex free energy landscape, thus accelerating folding. For a protein like SH3, where its folding nucleus is already specific and less diffuse, HI matters less at a temperature lower than the folding temperature. [u'Histological insight into the hepatic tissue of the Nile monitor (Varanus niloticus)', ['Yasser A. Ahmed', 'Mohammed Abdelsabour-Khalaf', 'Elsaysed Mohammed'], u'2018-01-31', u'The liver of reptiles is considered an important study model for the interaction between environment and hepatic tissue. Little is known about the histology of the liver of reptiles. The aim of the current study was to elucidate the histological architecture of the liver of the Nile monitor (Varanus niloticus). Liver fragments from the Nile monitor were collected in the summer season and processed for the light and electron microscopy. The liver of the Nile monitor was bi-lobed and the right lobe was found to be larger than the left lobe. Histological examination revealed indistinct lobulation of the liver, and the central vein, sinusoids and portal area were haphazardly organized. The hepatic parenchyma consisted of hepatocytes arranged in glandular-like alveoli or tubules separated by a network of twisted capillary sinusoids. The hepatocytes were polyhedral in shape with vacuolated cytoplasm and the nucleus was single rounded, eccentric, large and vesicular with a distinct nucleolus. The hepatocytes contained numerous lipid droplets, abundant glycogen granules and well-developed RER and mitochondria. The hepatocytes appeared to secrete into the bile canaliculi through the disintegration of their dark cytoplasm into the bile canaliculi. The space of Disse separating between the hepatocytes and sinusoids contained many recesses. The portal area contained branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct and lymphatic vessels embedded in a connective tissue. Some non-parenchymal cells were described such as Kupffer cells, heterophils, melano-macrophages, intercalated cells, myofibroblasts in addition to the endothelium of the sinusoids. This is the first report about the histological structure of the liver of the Egyptian Nile monitor.
